prime.problem: The natural recursion for fib(30) makes 2,692,537 calls to compute 31 different values, and each extra n multiplies the work by about 1.618. The same blow-up hides inside every hard problem on the source's Recursion page.
prime.fits: First card of the DP part. It turns the "handle each state once" idea from the graph cards into a cache or a table, and it gives the four-question checklist the next seven cards all answer.
expect: state = the numbers that pin a subproblem down
prime.goal: Turn a recursion into a memoized or tabulated DP, count its states, and decide from four questions whether DP applies at all.

attend: Why does naive fib(n) make 2F<sub>n+1</sub> − 1 calls when only n + 1 distinct values exist?
What exactly does a cache hit save: one call, or a whole subtree of calls?
Why does a bottom-up table need a fill order, and what guarantees each cell's inputs are ready?
In Coin Path, why is the state just the index i and not the path taken to reach it?
Why does @lru_cache hit the recursion limit at n = 498 while a plain dict reaches 998?

must: The recursion revisits the same subproblems through different call paths → store each answer the first time → every repeat becomes an O(1) lookup that also prunes its whole subtree → cost = states × work per state (31 states, 59 calls for fib(30))
Bottom-up fills cells in an order where every dependency is already filled → no recursion, so no 1,000-frame limit → and rows you're done with can be dropped (fib_two: O(1) space)
State = the few numbers that decide the rest of the problem, nothing about how you got there → Coin Path's state is the index i, not the path → a small state is what makes subproblems repeat
DP needs overlap + optimal substructure → disjoint halves (merge sort) never repeat, so a cache just costs memory; "everything chosen so far" states never repeat either → backtracking instead
elevated: A cold top-down call recurses n deep before anything is cached → deep inputs raise RecursionError even with a cache → warm the cache in increasing order, or tabulate
reference: Binet's formula first failing at n = 71

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the fib(5) call tree, circle the calls a cache removes, and write the four DP-spotting questions with fib's answer to each.
checklist: naive: 15 calls; memo: 9 calls (6 computed, 3 hits), 6 never made
optimal substructure: the answer is built from the parts' answers (a sum for counting)

retrieve.q: Explain why a cache turns fib's exponential running time into linear, in terms of what a hit prevents.
answer: a hit returns at once instead of making two more calls
so the entire subtree under that call is never explored
only n + 1 misses do real work, each O(1)

retrieve.q: Walk through Coin Path on [1, 2, 4, −1, 2], jump ≤ 2, filled from the end: cost and next at each cell.
Top-down with @lru_cache or bottom-up table: which do you write first in an interview, and what forces a switch?
answer: top-down first: the recursion plus a decorator, visits only needed states
switch when n can exceed about 500–1,000 (recursion limit), or to drop old rows for O(1)/O(n) space

compare.q: Both explore a tree of choices recursively. Which property of the subproblems decides whether you cache (DP) or prune (backtracking), and which problems need listing rather than counting?
answer: DP: the same small state recurs, so caching merges many paths
backtracking: the state includes everything chosen so far, so nothing recurs
listing every solution (Expression Add Operators) can't be cached away; counting or optimising usually can

compare.q: Merge sort also recurses on smaller inputs. Why does adding a cache to it do nothing useful, while it transforms fib?
answer: merge sort's subproblems are disjoint halves, each solved once anyway
fib's subproblems overlap: fib(n − 1) and fib(n − 2) share almost everything
overlap, not recursion, is what DP exploits

predict.q: Naive fib(30) makes 2,692,537 calls. Predict the call count for naive fib(35) and roughly how much longer it takes, before computing.
predict.answer: 2F<sub>36</sub> − 1 = 2 × 14,930,352 − 1 = 29,860,703 calls, about 11.1× as many (1.618⁵ ≈ 11.09). At the measured 0.129 s for fib(30), expect roughly 1.4 s. The memo version goes from 59 to 69 calls (2n − 1).

apply.task: Climbing Stairs with steps of 1, 2 or 3: write ways(n) as a recursion with base cases ways(n < 0) = 0 and ways(0) = 1, count its calls for n = 10, then add @lru_cache and read cache_info(). Finally write it bottom-up keeping only three variables.
apply.done: ways(10) = 274; the naive version makes 979 calls; the cached version reports 13 misses (states −2 … 10) and 18 hits; your three-variable loop also returns 274.
apply.hint: Count calls with a global counter incremented on entry, including the calls that hit a base case.

reflect: Could you explain "overlapping subproblems" with a picture instead of a definition?
Which prediction did you get wrong: the fib(35) count, or the memo's 69 calls?
Which link is fuzzy: small state → repeats, or repeats → cache pays off?
Which of the four questions is hardest for you to answer on a new problem?
What will you look for first on the two-strings card: the state or the fill order?
